title: Joshua's Farewell: Hold Fast to the LORD
summary: Old and near death, Joshua gathers Israel's leaders and reminds them that the LORD has fought for them and kept every promise. He charges them to obey the Law of Moses, to keep apart from the gods of the nations still in the land, and to love the LORD. He warns that if they turn to those nations and their gods, the same God who kept his good promises will keep his warnings too, and they will perish from the good land.
story: Joshua is the last of the generation that saw the Jordan open and Jericho fall, apart from Caleb. The land has been divided among the tribes, but, as chapter 13 admitted, much of it still has to be taken, and Canaanite peoples remain among Israel. Joshua 23 and 24 are two farewell scenes that close the book. This first one is a speech to the leaders about the future: what will keep Israel in the land, and what will cost them the land. It looks backward to Deuteronomy, where Moses gave a similar farewell, and forward to Judges, which opens with Joshua's death and shows his warnings coming true almost at once.
historical:
The chapter is set a long time after the rest from Israel's enemies, when Joshua is old, in the last years of his life (24:29 gives his age at death as 110). No place is named for this gathering, unlike the assembly at Shechem in chapter 24. The speech assumes the situation Joshua and Judges both describe: the major Canaanite powers broken in battle, but many towns and peoples still in the land, especially along the coast, in the valleys, and in pockets of the hill country. The nations that remain are not named here; the concern is less with military conquest than with what living next to these peoples will do to Israel's faith.

The list of those summoned (elders, leaders, judges, and officers) describes the tribal leadership of a society without a king. The elders were the heads of households and clans; the judges settled disputes; the officers seem to have been administrators who carried out orders, as in the army (Joshua 1:10).
cultural:
To call on a god's name or swear by it (verse 7) was to acknowledge that god's power and to place oneself under its protection. Oaths in the ancient world were sworn in the name of the gods who would punish the one who broke them. To swear by Baal was to treat Baal as real and as a guardian of one's word. Joshua forbids even this, not only sacrifice and bowing down.

Marriage in the ancient Near East bound families together, and it brought the gods of both families into the household. That is why Joshua names intermarriage as a danger (verse 12), echoing Deuteronomy 7:3-4, which explains that such marriages would turn Israel's children away from the LORD. The concern is religious, not ethnic: Rahab the Canaanite and Ruth the Moabite were welcomed into Israel when they turned to the LORD. The images of verse 13 (a snare, a trap, a whip, thorns) come from hunting and from the pain of a wound that won't heal, and they echo Moses' warning in Numbers 33:55.
literary: The chapter is almost entirely speech, in the style of Deuteronomy, and it follows the pattern of other great farewell addresses in Scripture: Moses in Deuteronomy, Samuel in 1 Samuel 12, and David in 1 Kings 2. Many scholars have noticed that it also follows the shape of ancient treaties between kings and vassals: a review of what the great king has done, the obligations of loyalty, and the blessings and curses that follow. The speech moves in two waves. Verses 3 to 13 review what the LORD has done and charge Israel to cling to him, ending with a warning. Verses 14 to 16 restate the same logic more sharply: every good word has come true, so every threatened word will come true as well. The repeated phrase "the LORD your God" appears again and again, and the verb to cling or hold fast (verses 8 and 12) is used for both loyalty to God and attachment to the nations. Israel will cling to one or the other.

outline.t: The LORD has fought for you and will finish the work
Keep the Law and do not serve the nations' gods
One can rout a thousand, so love the LORD
The danger of clinging to the nations
Every promise kept, every warning sure

doctrines.note: Joshua presents Israel's life in the land as covenant life: God has acted and promised, and Israel is called to answer with love and obedience. Breaking the covenant by serving other gods will bring the covenant curses.
Verses 14 and 15 rest on God's faithfulness. The God who never let one good promise fail is equally reliable in his warnings. His faithfulness is a comfort and a solemn caution at once.
The chapter traces how idolatry starts: not with a dramatic choice to abandon the LORD, but with friendship, marriage, and oaths that slowly draw a people into the worship of their neighbors.

words.note: Davaq, to cling or hold fast. It is used in Genesis 2:24 of a man holding fast to his wife, and in Deuteronomy of Israel's loyalty to God. Joshua uses it twice: Israel must hold fast to the LORD (verse 8) and not cling to the nations (verse 12). The word pictures a relationship of close attachment, and the chapter asks which attachment will win.

Naphal, to fall; here used for a promise that fails or falls to the ground unfulfilled. Joshua says twice in verse 14 that not one good word the LORD spoke has fallen. The same assurance closes the land division in 21:45.

Berit, covenant, the binding relationship God established with Israel at Sinai, with its promises and obligations. To transgress it (verse 16) is literally to pass over or cross its boundaries. The whole speech is an appeal to stay inside those boundaries.

Pach, a bird trap or snare. Joshua's image is of something that looks harmless until it closes. The nations that remain will not seem dangerous, but they will catch Israel, which is exactly how Judges 2:3 later describes them.

christ: Joshua's farewell rests on God keeping his word, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom all God's promises find their yes (2 Corinthians 1:20). Joshua could lead Israel into the land but could not keep them faithful there; his warnings fell on a people who would soon break the covenant. Hebrews 4:8 observes that if Joshua had given the people rest, God would not have spoken later of another day, and it points to a rest that remains for the people of God. The call to hold fast to the LORD echoes in the New Testament's call to hold fast to Christ and his word (Hebrews 10:23). The connection is thematic: the chapter shows the need for a faithfulness that Israel could not supply on its own.

hard.q: Doesn't the ban on intermarriage sound like ethnic prejudice?
hard.a: Read on its own, it can. But the reason given, here and in Deuteronomy 7, is religious: such marriages would turn Israel away from the LORD to other gods. The same Old Testament tells of Rahab and Ruth, foreign women who became part of Israel and of the line of David, because they turned to Israel's God. Some readers still find the command hard and see it as tied to Israel's particular situation of forming a nation in a land full of other gods. Most Christian interpreters see its lasting principle in Paul's concern that believers not bind themselves in marriage to those who do not share their faith (1 Corinthians 7:39), rather than in any ethnic rule.

questions: Joshua warns that the danger will not come from armies but from gradual attachment to the nations' ways. What slow attachments pull people away from God today?
Verse 14 says not one of God's promises had failed. How does remembering God's past faithfulness shape how you face the future?
Why do you think Joshua insists that God's warnings are as sure as his promises? Is that comforting, frightening, or both?
